vignette:
Lien presents as a meticulously composed woman of seventy-one, her professional demeanor as a financial analyst a stark contrast to the profound internal disarray she describes. For decades, she managed to compartmentalise the past, but in the last year, following her retirement, the walls she had so carefully constructed have begun to crumble. She came to therapy after her daughter, visiting from out of state, found her awake at 4 a.m., staring at a blank television screen, and refused to leave until Lien made an appointment.

The trauma occurred nearly fifty years ago, in the aftermath of the fall of Saigon. As a university student, Lien was sent to a "re-education" camp, a year of captivity that she speaks of in fragmented, hushed tones. The narrative is not one of dramatic violence, but of slow, grinding degradation: the constant hunger, the filth that clung to everything, the arbitrary cruelty of the guards, and the gnawing uncertainty of her fate. What haunts her most is the memory of being utterly abandoned. No institution-not her government, not international aid, not the world she had read about-came to her aid. The nights were the worst, a time when disappearances happened, when the thin walls of the barracks offered no protection from the sounds of suffering or the sudden beam of a flashlight.

This history has calcified into a set of core beliefs that now govern her life. Her conviction that the people and systems meant to protect her had fundamentally failed has generalised into a worldview of profound institutional betrayal. This, combined with a deep, pervasive sense of being contaminated by the filth and humiliation of the camp, has led her to see the world as an inherently dangerous place. She has come to believe she is incapable of dealing with even the slightest upset, that she lacks the fortitude to navigate a world she perceives as treacherous. As a result of these appraisals, her sense of safety has shrunk to the confines of her small, obsessively tidy apartment. This is the only place she feels a semblance of control; the world outside is a source of unpredictable threat.

This pervasive sense of threat, which crests with the setting sun, drives her into a rigid, defensive routine. The belief that she is uniquely unsafe at night, a direct echo of the camp, has made sleep an enemy. To avoid the vulnerability of unconsciousness, Lien began to delay sleep, staying up until she was on the verge of collapse. She would spend hours at her desk, not working, but trying to exhaust her mind with old case files or complex financial models. This was a deliberate strategy to keep her thoughts at bay; she actively tries to push away any flicker of memory from that year, believing that if she lets one in, the rest will follow and overwhelm her completely.

These strategies, however, have become a cage of their own. The forced wakefulness and thought suppression do not bring peace. The exhaustion from sleeping only three or four hours a night has frayed her nerves, cementing her belief that she is incapable of handling even the slightest upset. The late-night hours, intended to be a distraction, have instead become a theater for counterfactual thinking, where she endlessly replays how her life would have been different, how much she has lost. This state of perpetual exhaustion, a direct result of her efforts to keep watch, paradoxically leaves her feeling even more vulnerable during the day, heightening her baseline sense of threat. The sheer intensity of her fear, in turn, serves as daily proof of her own brokenness. She feels a constant, low-grade shame, a sense of being fundamentally soiled by her past.

The trigger for seeking help was mundane. A notice about scheduled maintenance in her apartment building, requiring workers to enter her unit, sent her into a multi-day panic. The thought of strangers in her only safe zone was intolerable. For two days, she barely ate, consumed by fear and the powerful, negative feelings of horror and anger that the intrusion provoked. It was in this state that her daughter found her. Lien admits she feels trapped, not by walls and wire anymore, but by her own mind. Her hope for therapy is simple, and she states it with the quiet desperation of someone who has been fighting a long, losing battle: she wants to feel safe enough to turn the lights off at night.
